source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, Table 1 re-opened (ICLR 2026 version v3)
finding: Re-read of the 20 Questions table. The 18 for 'ICL Beliefs' comes from skipping the hypothesis-filtering step when building the belief, not from a poorly estimated EIG formula. The EIG estimator itself (BED-LLM) is best. Predictive entropy (Entropy) is the strongest alternative.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Animals, success % after 20 turns: Prompt-Only 44, BED-LLM 88, Entropy 79, Data-Estimation 64, Implicit Maximization (LLM picks the best question by judgement) 47, ICL Beliefs 18. GPT-4o Animals: Prompt-Only 45, BED-LLM 93. 100 targets per set, standard errors about 2 to 5 points.
quote: BED-LLM comfortably outperforms all alternative approaches
limits: Column labels in the extracted table are scrambled; the mapping of values to methods follows the paper's text (ICL Beliefs worst, Entropy best alternative). Claim K12 should say 'bad belief construction', not 'bad EIG estimator'. Answerer is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Two lessons: the belief over hypotheses must be filtered to be consistent with all answers so far; and asking the model to 'pick the most informative question' (47) loses to computing EIG over sampled hypotheses (88).

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, appendix on hypothesis count and settings
finding: Sample counts used and how many are enough. The ranking of candidate questions is stable with about 10 sampled hypotheses even though the EIG values keep moving until about 85.
numbers: 20 Questions main runs: at least N=15 hypotheses (up to 3 sample-then-filter rounds), M=15 candidate questions. Preference elicitation: N=5 hypotheses, M=8 candidates. Fig 10: one game, turn 5, five candidate questions, GPT-4o-mini; order at |Theta|=10 equals order at |Theta|=85.
limits: Sensitivity check is one game, one turn, five questions. Not a general result. Number of imagined answers (the y samples) is not swept; only the hypothesis count.
agent_relevance: A working budget for an EIG-style question choice: about 10 to 15 consistent hypotheses and about 8 to 15 candidate questions. Absolute EIG value is not needed, only the ranking.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, Table 3 wall-clock
finding: Full EIG costs about the same as plain entropy because the conditional-entropy term reuses the same likelihood calls. Data-Estimation (the other way to build a joint model) is over ten times slower.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B, whole Animals set: BED-LLM runtime comparable to or slightly below Entropy and Split; Data-Estimation more than one order of magnitude slower; Prompt-Only and CoT cheapest (one call per turn).
limits: Wall-clock, not tokens. Exact seconds were not copied. Equal-token comparison against Prompt-Only is not given.
agent_relevance: Cheapest estimator that beats entropy: the prior-likelihood EIG (sample hypotheses, ask the model for P(answer | hypothesis), mix). It adds almost no cost over entropy.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, film preference task and model mismatch
finding: With a real mismatch between questioner and answerer model families, BED-LLM helps most. Prompt-Only is a stronger baseline here than in 20 Questions.
numbers: Mean rating of 10 recommended films, 200 users from MovieLens-100K profiles written by o3; answerers and questioners drawn from GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large, Qwen2.5-72B; ratings roughly 3.5 to 4.5.
quote: BED-LLM's benefit is most clear in scenarios where the questioner belongs to a different model class
limits: Still simulated users (LLM answerers built from ratings). Gain sizes are small on the 1 to 5 rating scale and were read from a figure.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly: benefit survives a different-model answerer, but no real human in the loop was tested.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information, Table 1 and Table 2 re-read
finding: Cost sweep re-read. Table 1 (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Mixed 20Q) shows VoI beating the best tuned baseline at the three low costs and losing at the two high ones. At c=0.20 the best policy is to ask nothing.
numbers: Utility, VoI vs best baseline: c=0.01 8.64 vs 8.30 (+0.34); c=0.02 7.72 vs 6.88 (+0.84); c=0.05 5.01 vs 3.65 (+1.36); c=0.10 1.38 vs 2.28 (-0.90, best is Confidence 0.5); c=0.20 -0.96 vs 0 (-0.96, best is No Question). Main text gives 14.14 vs 11.49 at c=0.01 for Mixed 20Q, a different run (appendix row VOI 0.01 = 14.14).
limits: Table 1 and the main-text 14.14 vs 11.49 are different runs. Which model carries 14.14 was not settled from the text. One task, one model in the cost sweep. Baselines tuned on the same data.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: with cost near 10 to 20 percent of the maximum gain per question, a no-ask rule or a tuned confidence threshold beats VoI. VoI lost because its own belief overstated the gain (it kept asking at negative utility).

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information, calibration analysis
finding: Calibration is only checked by argmax accuracy vs truth, not by a proper scoring rule. The authors say the models are reasonably calibrated on animal guessing and less so on medical diagnosis, yet VoI still matched the best baselines in most settings at costs 0.01 and 0.05.
numbers: Calibration figure (GPT-4 and Gemini-2.5-Flash). Headline wins are at c=0.01 and c=0.05 in Figure 2; the sweep to c=0.10 and 0.20 exists only for one model/task (Table 1).
limits: No calibration level was varied on purpose, so the question 'what calibration makes no-ask best' is not answered by this paper. Only the cost axis was swept.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays partly open: the cost threshold is seen (about 0.10 on a 0 to 9 utility scale), the calibration threshold is not.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts, Appendix E simulation depth
finding: Depth 1 (one-step, myopic, still using the information-gain reward) already gives most of the gain. Depth 3 adds a little to a lot depending on task.
numbers: Success % at depth 1, 2, 3: 20 Questions 82.6, 86.7, 92.5; the other two series (read from figure) 66.1, 67.0, 75.2 and 63.5, 64.7, 67.3. Depth 3 vs depth 1: +9.9, +9.1, +3.8 points.
limits: Figure values with unclear series labels (20Q is the top series; which of the two lower ones is medical and which is troubleshooting was inferred, troubleshooting 67.3 matches the main table). Not token-matched across depth. Depth 3 was chosen for budget, deeper not tried. Closed hypothesis set and simulated answerer.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a myopic one-step information-gain rule keeps 60 to 90 percent of the depth-3 gain on these tasks. Interacting tests (where one test only pays off after another) are not tested here.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Collaborative Battleship
finding: Humans (N=42, 126 games) and 15 LMs compared with an exact Bayesian ideal. Sampling candidate questions and keeping the one with the highest EIG lifts weak models above humans when combined with Bayesian move choice. A one-step lookahead decision rule (ask vs shoot, DBayes) adds a small further gain.
numbers: Captain F1: Llama-4-Scout LM 0.367, +Bayes-Q 0.393, +Bayes-M 0.685, +Bayes-QM 0.741, +Bayes-QMD 0.764; GPT-4o 0.450, 0.471, 0.727, 0.753, 0.782; GPT-5 LM 0.716, with +Bayes-QM 0.722. Human 0.615 F1, 8.2 questions, EIG median 0.411 vs ceiling 0.531 bits. Win rate 0.67 vs GPT-5 for the full-Bayes weaker models at 1% (Llama-4-Scout) and 35% (GPT-4o) of GPT-5's cost. QBayes cut redundant (zero-EIG) questions 18.5% to 0.2% (Llama), 14.6% to 1.2% (GPT-4o).
limits: Board game with a fixed grid hypothesis space; spotter fixed to GPT-5 with noise epsilon=0.1. Higher EIG alone barely raised F1 (+0.021 to +0.026 for Q only); the gain came from using the answer well (M). GPT-5 itself did not benefit.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 6: more sampled candidate questions give more EIG (up to 94.2% of the ceiling at 10 samples). A one-step ask-or-act rule helped by +0.023 to +0.029 F1 on top of the Bayes question and move steps. Strong reasoning models may already do this implicitly.

source: Grand et al. (2026) Battleship, Guess Who? replication and spotter accuracy
finding: The answerer is the weak link. Spotter accuracy for a noisy answerer ranged from near chance to above human. The method replicated on a second game.
numbers: Human spotter accuracy 92.5% on 931 gold questions (simple 92.8%, complex 91.9%). 15 LMs from 52.5% (GPT-4o-mini) to 92.8% (o3-mini). GPT-4o 72.8% simple to 60.4% complex; Llama-4-Scout 68.0% to 54.0%. Code generation +13.2 points, CoT plus code +14.7. Guess Who?: +28.3 to +42.4 points accuracy.
limits: The captain study fixes the spotter to GPT-5 and sets noise epsilon=0.1 from its accuracy. With a weaker answerer the ideal Bayes rule would need a larger epsilon. Humans were collaborators, not a noisy test with a known rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the EIG gain assumes an answer-noise parameter. The paper does model it (epsilon), which is the sensitivity/specificity idea, but only one value was run in the captain tests.

source: Ding, Tomlin, Durrett (2026) Calibrate-Then-Act, Table 2 re-opened
finding: Pandora's Box with Qwen3-8B. Giving priors without thinking mode did nothing useful; thinking plus priors reached near-optimal. Thinking without priors was also weak. The paper only toggles thinking on or off.
numbers: 100 examples, K=3, discount from 0 to 1 in 0.1 steps, Dirichlet(0.5) priors. Optimal-match %: oracle 100, Prompted-NonThink 11, Prompted (think, no priors) 23, CTA-NonThink (priors, no thinking) 20, CTA-Prompted (priors, think) 94. Reward: 0.649, 0.441, 0.476, 0.436, 0.625.
limits: One 8B model, one toy task, binary thinking switch. No intermediate reasoning budget was tested, so the smallest budget that unlocks the effect is unknown. Trace analysis says the non-thinking model verifies all options and does not compare expected gain with cost.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: stating prior and cost without any reasoning does not help (20% match; reward 0.436, below the 0.476 of thinking without priors). A cheap EV check needs explicit reasoning steps, not just more context.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Budget-Aware Tool Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling (Budget Tracker, BATS)
finding: Equal-budget test of telling the agent how many tool calls are left. Plain ReAct agents stop gaining past a ceiling when given more budget. A budget signal gives better accuracy at the same budget and the same accuracy for less cost. Includes a coding agent test.
numbers: Web search agents: at budget 10 Avg@4 rose from 47.8% to 55.5% (one model); Budget Tracker at budget 10 matched ReAct at budget 100 using 40.4% fewer search calls and 31.3% lower cost (12.8% vs 12.6% on BrowseComp). SWE agent at budget 50: resolve rate 55.4% vs 36.8% with similar calls (45.7 vs 46.0) and similar token cost; also beat the budget-60 baseline (55.4% vs 53.2%) with 9.9% fewer calls.
limits: This is cost awareness, not an EVSI gate. No value estimate is made. Gains might come from the agent stopping earlier rather than from a better value judgement.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (adjacent): the closest equal-budget, coding-agent evidence. A simple 'budget left' line beats larger raw budgets. A value-gated rule has not been compared against it.

source: Qian et al. (2025) SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation
finding: LLM agents call tools on questions they can answer without them (tool overuse). Overuse sometimes causes wrong answers. Training on rationales for when a tool is needed cut calls by 24% and raised performance 37% (macro average).
numbers: GSM8K preliminary: Llama-3.1-8B overuse rate above 50%; LLMs call tools unnecessarily over 30% of the time. SMARTAgent: 24.0% fewer tool uses, 37.1% better performance (macro averages), unnecessary calls cut by up to 50% vs prompting with tool access; OOD GSM8K/MINTQA kept accuracy with one fifth of the tool calls.
limits: Overuse is defined as calling a tool on a question the model solves correctly alone, not as 'information that cannot change the decision'. It is a training fix, not a prompt check. No 'could this change my answer?' prompt was tried.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (closest LLM analog): the waste-on-useless-information pattern exists in agents (30% to 50%+ of cases), and it can hurt accuracy. The Bastardi and Shafir shift of choice is not tested.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Position: Agents Should Invoke External Tools Only When Epistemically Necessary
finding: A position paper that names unnecessary tool calls as a failure mode and argues for a necessity check before acting. Only the opening pages were read; it gives no measured test of such a check.
numbers: No measured results in the pages read; used as a framing source.
limits: Opinion, not data. Authors overlap with the SMART paper. Only first pages read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: no study found that tests a 'could this change my decision?' prompt on LLM agents. The literature offers the idea and the problem, not the measured fix.

source: Kleinberg and Marsh (2023) Less is more: information needs, information wants (Cogn Res Princ Implic 8:57)
finding: Human decision study that builds on Bastardi and Shafir (1998). Extra causal information beyond what the target choice needs lowered accuracy, and people who chose the most complex diagram did worst. Not a replication of the 1998 paradigm.
numbers: Five experiments (online samples, hypothetical decisions for others). Experiment 5 accuracy by chosen info level: none 0.64 (women) / 0.59 (men), simple 0.80 / 0.73, simple-plus 0.76 / 0.69, complex 0.69 / 0.59. Only 14% chose the complex model. A small amount of extra information (simple-plus) already cut the share choosing the target answer.
limits: Extension of the idea, not the same task. Decisions were hypothetical and for another person. Mechanism: people did not know which parts of the information were relevant.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 side: supports that surplus information harms decisions and that people do not pick well what they need. Not a preregistered replication of Bastardi and Shafir.

source: Chandrashekar et al. (2021) Accentuation and compatibility: preregistered replication of Shafir (1993), Judgment and Decision Making
finding: A preregistered close replication of a sister Shafir effect (choosing vs rejecting) failed in most problems. It shows that Shafir-style effects from the 1990s do not always survive large online samples. It is not about useless information.
numbers: N=1,026 American MTurk participants, 8 problems. Same direction as original in 2 problems (4 and 5, d=0.26 to 0.45), opposite in 2 (7 and 8, d=-0.22 to -0.53), null with Bayes factors favouring null in 4. Pooled d=-0.01 [-0.06, 0.03]; original d=0.32 and 0.38. Accentuation account fit better.
limits: Different paradigm from Bastardi and Shafir. The original author (Shafir and Cheek 2024) disputes how close the replication was. Stimuli date from the 1990s.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: raises the base rate for failed replication of Shafir-lab effects. No preregistered or large-N replication of the 1998 useless-information task was found in this search (search tools were rate limited), so K08 should stay contested and thinly supported.

source: The effect of noninstrumental information on reward learning (2024) Memory and Cognition 52, PMC11315740
finding: Two experiments with money at stake and learned (not described) payoffs. People gave up reward to get advance information about an outcome they could not change. The preference was not caused by a wrong picture of the payoffs.
numbers: Two-armed bandit with 'Find Out Now' vs 'Keep It Secret' options; the informative option was the lower-paying one. Participants still took it at a cost in points; reward estimates were similar with and without advance information. Exact sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Tests paying for non-instrumental information (curiosity), not the Bastardi and Shafir shift in choice. Abstract and design text read; statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: real-money incentives do not remove the pull of useless information (conceptual replication, 2024). Boundary: the effect here is willingness to pay, not a changed decision.

source: Computed for this gap search: exact Bayes EVSI and EVPI for a binary test with sensitivity and specificity
finding: Own calculation (not a source read). Binary state, act or not act, utility +B if act when present, -C if act when absent, 0 if not act. EVSI is zero unless a test result can move the belief across the act threshold C/(B+C). Closed form when the prior is below the threshold: EVSI = max(0, p*sens*B - (1-p)*(1-spec)*C). EVPI = p*B, the upper cap.
numbers: B=C=1 (threshold 0.5): p=0.10 sens=spec=0.9 gives EVPI 0.100, EVSI 0 (belief after a positive result reaches only 0.50); p=0.20 gives EVSI 0.100 (50% of EVPI); p=0.30 EVSI 0.200 (67%); p=0.50 EVSI 0.400 (80%). p=0.30: sens=spec 0.6 or 0.7 gives EVSI 0 (belief after positive 0.39 and 0.50), 0.8 gives 0.100 (33%). p=0.50 sens=spec 0.99 gives 0.490 (98%). With C=4 (threshold 0.8) and p=0.30 sens=spec=0.9: EVSI 0 (belief after positive 0.794, below 0.8).
limits: Toy two-state case; no test cost subtracted (net value = EVSI - cost). Not from Raiffa and Schlaifer or Howard directly (book not opened). Agrees with the standard result that EVSI <= EVPI and with a01.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 and 2 (rule of thumb): a test is worth buying only if the belief after the most favourable result crosses the decision threshold, which needs LR+ greater than odds(threshold)/odds(prior). EVSI is then capped by EVPI. An LLM can be checked against this table.

source: Ren et al. (2023) KnowNo: Robots That Ask For Help, answerer assumption
finding: Conformal prediction triggers a help request when the prediction set has more than one option. The answerer in the method and proof is assumed to give correct help.
numbers: Simulation 200 trials per setting, target success level 0.85; hardware experiments also run.
limits: Text states the assumption that the human faithfully provides help. The human in tests is an experimenter or simulator. Noisy or wrong answers are not studied.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the answerer is idealised even here. Real-user noise stays an unmeasured factor.
